en: Attention has been paid to the *śuddhipattra* (pp. 327–8) as well as to Mme Brunner’s corrections (1985: 424–9), a number of which derive from manuscripts that were not available to Bhatt.

Having prostrated before that Lord, we compose this exposition on the *Caryāpāda*—He by whom the stainless nature of the atoms, known as perception and action, has been obscured; through whose existence the multitude of living beings falls into the ocean of worldly existence; and by whose grace one destroys that darkness which is so difficult to ward off.
Now, therefore, the summary of the general conduct for the spiritual guides and others, which is further relevant to the present occasion, is taught in brief. (MṛgT 3.1)
The teacher, the one who practices the mantra, the spiritual son, and the initiate—these four are Śaivas, whether they observe the vows or not. (Mṛgendra-tantra 3.2)
Those who observe vows are either matted-haired, shaven-headed, or smeared white with ashes; among them, the foremost are kings and others adorned with sectarian marks, forehead streaks, and turbans.
A Śūdra should not wear matted locks, nor should one who is ignorant, nor one who is negligent;
nor should a woman, nor one who has not reached the proper age, nor one who is diseased, nor even one who is physically impaired.
Having divided the hair according to the number of the Kalās, Tattvas, Pavitras, Aṇus, Śaktis, Mantras, and Īśas, and having sprinkled it, one should apply the Saṃhitā-mantras to each portion.
In front of Vrateśvara, one should bind [the thread] with the splendor of Śiva:
for the mantra-practitioner (mantrin) with the *sādhya-mantra*, and for the *putraka* and the *yogya* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (MṛgT 3.6)

One who observes the vow of the Bhūtas should bring those [images] to completion by means of ash mixed with anthelmintic substances, or with the three myrobalans (triphalā), or with powdered iron. Mṛgendratantra 3.7.
Those whose vow is limited are considered practitioners of material vows;
those for whom it lasts until the fall of the body are known as practitioners of the ultimate vow.
The gurus and those who are spiritual sons (*putraka*) are not beginners (*prāthamikasādhaka*);
they have correctly completed the full extent of the observance (*pūrṇavrata*) and have offered their vows to the Lord of Vows (*vrateśa*).
One who has laid down the limbs of the vow, yet possesses the splendor of taking a virtuous wife, is called a *bhautika* or a *kāmya*, or indeed a *satsāntānika*. (MṛgT 3.10)

The practitioner who follows worldly conventions, the spiritual son, the one who has performed the ritual bath, the householder, and the initiate who was previously a householder—these Śaivas may be devoid of [specific] vows. (MṛgT 3.11)
Their common duties are the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana), ritual adoration (arcana), bathing, and so forth; on the sacred festival days (parvan), these rites are performed with double intensity.

Alms-food from the four castes, provided it is not contemptible, may be eaten from leaves of the *nyagrodha* or *aśvattha* trees, from leaves of the *vātaghna* tree, or from a bronze vessel. Mṛgāra 3.13.
In the consecration of bridges and other such works, in the installation of all the deities of the immortals,
and in the purificatory rites beginning with the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), there is the avoidance of cooked food.

On the fourteenth, the eighth, and the fifteenth days, one should subsist on sacrificial food, or on fruits and roots, or on some other suitable offering fit for the sacrificial fire. Mṛgatīrtha 3.15.
On days of Vyatīpāta, during the destruction of a lunar day (dhvaṃsa), in months of intercalary days (māsavṛddhi), at the solstices (ayana), and so forth,
special self-restraint must be observed and the Śaivas must be gratified with offerings.
When a Śiva-yogin is exhausted on the road, overwhelmed by enemies, afflicted by disease, or tormented by hunger,
one must rescue him with all one's being.
The renunciation of meat, women, and honey; sleeping on the ground for one who observes the vow;
guarding one's mother alone; and being accompanied by a single water-pot. (Mṛgāputra-kathā 3.18)

One should disregard the songs, dances, conversations, and amorous gestures of women; one should not remain in private with a woman; and one should avoid wearing garlands, anointing the body with oil, and similar luxuries. (Mṛgatīrtha 3.19)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, on the eighth, when the Siddhas are visible,
on all festival days (parvan), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), and during the Aṣṭakās and other such occasions, one should perform the Śrāddha rite.
One should honor one's elder brothers— who are like teachers and equal to kinsmen—
with offerings such as the *madhuparka* at the appropriate times, and one should attend to one's wife.
The practice of auspicious conduct and the wearing of perfumes, garlands, and so forth—
these various modes of conduct for each of them are likewise prescribed.
The Guru, being diligent, should bestow grace upon those impelled by the power of Maheśa, having thoroughly discerned them through the tests prescribed by the elders. (MṛgT 3.23)
Since one becomes liable for expiation by failing to perform [the rite] for devotees of Śiva and by performing it for those who are unfaithful,
one should therefore exert effort beyond this.

For an initiated woman who has committed adultery, one should perform the rite of revivification (*saṃjīvana*) through the *sṛṣṭi* [mantra], accompanied by the *saṃhitā-homa* and the concluding full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). (MṛgT 3.25)
There is no reviving for a burnt action once it has been falsely accumulated;
rather, that which pacifies the exhaustion and downfall [of such action] is the penance (prāyaścitta) prescribed by the Guru.
For those followers who have fallen from their positions in other philosophical systems,
one should first establish them in the limit of their own innate nature and then perform initiation in reverse order.
Those who employ mantras are not considered to be subject to rebirth;
therefore, through the complete accomplishment of mantra-sādhana, one should perform those other [deeds].
Free from envy, one should explain the meaning of the Tantra to the devotees of Śiva who abide in the right path,
while protecting the lineage of the gurus according to the proper method.
Not when there is indigestion or the belching of sour tastes, nor during the obstruction of feces or urine;
not during vomiting or diarrhea, nor while unclean, nor after sexual intercourse.

Standing upon the purified surface of the earth, which is free from the hearing of animals, and having worshipped Śiva— who is situated within the enclosure and whose form is the Praṇava— Mṛgendratantra 3.31.
Having placed the leader of the community, the Guru, the officiant, the one who is the locus of the ritual action, and the book containing the secret, true Sūtras above someone [else], MṛgT 3.32.

The teacher, facing east or north, should say, "Come, recite," and once the student has achieved his purpose, he should begin the exposition preceded by a statement of the connection and the subject matter. (Mṛgatantre 3.33)

One should speak of the stream, the divisions following the stream, and their enumeration; one should speak of the source and oneself for the sake of practice, for by failing to mention them, one would be a thief. (Mṛgatantre 3.34)
The channels beginning with Kāmikā lead upwards; those beginning with Asitāṅga are on the right;
those beginning with Sammoha are on the left; and those beginning with Trotalā are extensive in the east. (Mṛgendratantra 3.35)

The Āpya [initiation], that which involves the blade of a fierce sword and so forth, that which is under the protection of Caṇḍanātha, the Śaiva, the Māntra, the Aiśvara, the Gāṇa, the Divya, the Ārṣa, and the Gauhyaka. MṛgT 3.36.
The wise know that there are eight currents, including the Yoginī, Siddha, and Kaula;
one should explain them individually according to their respective divisions, following the sequence of each current.
The Śaiva Prāktana-tantra is established by [Śiva’s] command, without a doubt;
it was created by his lords, the Gaṇas, the gods, and the sages, according to his will. (MṛgT 3.38)
Having understood through his own words that [the power] had been accumulated and had arrived under that very name, the Guhyakas, Bhujagas, Yakṣas, and Dānavas were impelled by Śiva. (MṛgT 3.39)
That which they spoke after withdrawing that stream is known as the *gauhyaka*;
through it, the yoginīs immediately attained the knowledge that illuminates yoga.

Because that Yoginīkula was not transmitted by anyone other than those very [goddesses], so too is any other [teaching] that is a withdrawal (saṃhāra); it is indeed a mixture when it is mixed. (MṛgT 3.41)
Because they are divided according to the differences among their proponents, there is no fixed number for them;
the Śaivas, Raudras, and Mahābhedas, as well as the ten and eighteen [Tantras], are located in the upper [direction]. (MṛgT 3.42)
The *Kāmika*, the first [tantra] of the Śaivas, which arises from yoga and is inconceivable, was uttered by Rudra through the Rudras possessed by Śiva, and not from their own intellect. (MṛgT 3.43)

The wise know the tenth [perfection] as follows: the cause (kāraṇa), the unconquered (ajita), the one called radiant (dīpta), the subtle (sūkṣma), the supreme (parama), the thousand-rayed (sāhasrāṃśumat), and the very luminous (suprabha). MṛgT 3.44.
First, the *Raudrāṇāṃvijaya*, then the *Niḥśvāsa* of the Supreme Lord (*Pārameśvara*), likewise the *Svāyambhuva*, the *Āgneya*, the *Vīrabhadra*, and the *Raurava*. (Mṛgendratantra 3.45)
The crown known as Vimala, and that called Candrajñāna;
the Mukhabimbaka, the Udgīta, the Lalita, and that designated as Siddha.
The *Santāna*, the *Śarva-ukta*, the *Kiraṇa*, and the supreme *Vātula*—one should not explain these at length on the first day, having begun them only after a long time. (MṛgT 3.47)
Even at the beginning, there is no excessive questioning or counter-questioning;
there are three root sūtras, or likewise two, or even one. (MṛgT 3.48)

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should thereafter desist; for if one speaks further, one is obstructed by impediments, where the great tree of the meaning of the Tantra has taken root like a seed. (MṛgT 3.49)
That root sūtra shines forth, adorned with the word "atha" and others;
there may be another [text] as its enumeration (uddeśaka), expressing numbers, technical names, and so forth. (MṛgT 3.50)
The definition of "tallakṣaṇa" is the statement of its essential nature; anything else is a summary of the commentary.
Both he who explains it thus and he who studies it have their defilements destroyed. (MṛgT 3.51)
Having attained radiant fame in the world, they shall enter the abode of Śiva;
for those who listen according to the procedure prescribed in their own tantra during non-study periods, [the merit] is in vain.
Speaking of Śaivism here, one becomes short-lived and, upon death, attains the state of a preta;
one should not teach on the fourteenth day or the eighth day of either fortnight. (MṛgT 3.53)
On the new moon and full moon days, on the fourth lunar day,
during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), and following a thunderclap, a meteor, or an earthquake, the day [is inauspicious] for archery.
And because these [omens] are seen during twilight, thunder, the burning of the quarters, halos, meteors, mist, the eastern rainbow, and in the sky or cities. (MṛgT 3.55)
When the sun and moon are situated in the *kīlaka* yoga, for three days; during the appearance of Rāhu (an eclipse);
for five nights during the sacrifice to Hari; and during the *pavitra* rite dedicated to the enemy of Makha (Śiva).
If a cat, a snake, or a frog has passed through [the water] during the day, one must wait for three days;
if a three-hooded serpent is seen, [one must wait] for three days, and if a two-hooded serpent is seen, for two days. (MṛgT 3.57)

On hearing the sound of a corpse within, upon burning, on the smell of a corpse, in a harsh wind, and when a well-known person dies—unless these have ceased—one should observe a day [of fasting]. (MṛgT 3.58)
When the Guru has become Śiva, [the impurity lasts] for one month; when a brother, a disciple, or the like, for three days;
when a king who follows the Śaiva path, for seven days; and when one who follows the path of the bound (paśu), for three nights.

The teacher, regarding those perfected beings who belong to his own lineage as well as others, should provide the initial exposition, subsequent reflection, resolution of doubts, and the final conclusion. (MṛgT 3.60)
Whether he be an initiate (*samayin*) or a spiritual son (*putraka*), having discovered something previously unknown,
he should, once authorized, report it to the Guru who resides at the sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
Or one who is consecrated by his own [guru] may hear it from the Lord Śaṅkara, the beloved of the seats of yoga (yogapīṭha),
whether he is situated externally or from one established externally, even from one consecrated by another who has not attained the seats.
One should not go anywhere without shoes, nor without a companion;
one should not go too far ahead, nor at the wrong time, nor at night, nor in the dust or the heat of the sun.
One should not dwell with the lowly, nor should one wander aimlessly from house to house;
likewise, one should not mock anyone, nor imitate them, nor cause them harm.
Since that guru would not perform any improper conduct, his lack of authority in matters such as political counsel and the like is not prevented [by this]. (MṛgT 3.65)
Having risen in the morning, the spiritual son, having performed his daily rites as a practitioner of the observances (samayin),
and having offered salutations, should perform his duties with the permission of the Guru.
Having studied, one should listen to the scripture while remaining under the guidance of a teacher and dwelling with him,
having abandoned the continuous stream of pride, envy, hypocrisy, and addiction.
One should not clear one's throat, spit, cough, laugh, or the like in the presence of the guru; nor should one engage in debate with anyone while wearing superior attire.

Rubbing the body with unguents, personal grooming, yawning, remaining in postures, conversing on equal terms, assuming the paryanka cross-legged position, meditating, performing worship, and so forth. (Mṛgatantre 3.69)

A wise person should not offer salutation to one who is eating, one established in meditative concentration, one walking in meditation, one engaged in ritual activity, or one standing in the presence of the guru.
One should follow behind him as he walks and enter after him when he enters;
one should not question his words, nor should one wake him while he is sleeping.
Having been permitted, he may wander for alms; having obtained food, he should eat what has been offered;
he should sleep while others sleep, and so forth—he should perform whatever is enjoined by the rules.
Having been authorized, the spiritual son may act according to his desire or dwell in the [teacher's] abode;
as a householder who has previously entered the vow, he should serve the guru with diligence.
Since the category of the probandum has not yet been attained, its attainment must likewise depend upon that [substratum];
therefore, something residing in another locus cannot be its establisher.
The practitioner, authorized by his guru and having resorted to a sacred field,
should assume the guise of the one to be accomplished, observe silence, and subsist on sacrificial oblations, cooked rice, and vegetables.
Accompanied by a companion, remaining vigilant, and subsisting only on fruits and roots,
one should worship Śiva after performing the sacrifice and perform the recitation (japa) as prescribed in the three ways.
Having performed the oblation of the tenth part and bathed in the pitcher of that sacrifice on an auspicious day,
one situated in the sacred field (kṣetra) should begin the rite, or practice while taking refuge in spiritual perfection (siddhi).
One should not favor anyone, nor associate with them, nor reprimand them;
one should not sit elsewhere for long, except when there is the acquisition of a [meditation] field.
When half the day has passed at the time of the third libation,
one should practice the *mādhūkarī* alms-round for the sake of all mantras, which is meritorious and has the Supreme Lord as its presiding deity.
If one partakes of the libation honored by the Sūras without having first accomplished that [rite],
the mantras established upon the seat of yoga will not take up residence within him.
While wandering for alms, one should not accept alms from those who revile [the path],
nor from followers of Śiva, nor from those of the Svāyambhuva school, nor from any who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin).
One should not accept alms consisting of abundant sweet food, nor those that are overly refined, nor from a place where women are clever at jesting and the like. (MṛgT 3.82)
Having performed the protection ritual and remembering the weapon-mantra, he should wander about while observing silence;
if he does not obtain alms, he should feel neither anger nor should he hold onto it for long.
And while the [initiation] paths are being traversed, no one shall speak anything unpleasant;
nor shall one offer a portion to the teacher, the fire, Śiva, the Vidyā, or the Kṣetrapāla.

Having extracted [the substance] with an assistant and divided it, one who is pure should consume a portion on the ground; then, having sipped water for purification, one should recite the mantra during the Vaiṣṇava observance.

When that has passed, one should offer an oblation preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* with the mantra "To the Guardian of the Field, Svāhā," and present the *bali* offering in the southwest, preceded by perfumes and incense.
Then, having spread out a good hide and assumed a posture without sloth, the wise man, meditating on the mantra, should recite it; when weary, he may sleep lightly upon it.
Having arisen at midnight, one should perform worship, recitation, and so forth;
thereafter, during the Brāhma-savana, one should fetch sacrificial fuel and other materials.
One should worship with supreme faith those Śaivas who have arrived at one's residence,
having recognized them as such by their characteristics and through the excellence of their ritual implements, according to what is appropriate.
One should not bow down to anyone, nor should one disclose the mantra to be accomplished to anyone;
one should not cast away medicinal herbs, mantras, cows, Brahmins, or ascetics.
These are the places where Śiva manifests; since they are indeed censurers of Śiva, one should worship Śaṅkara on the festival days with an especially distinguished offering.
One should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) to the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla) and the deity to be accomplished (sādhya), and not to anyone else;
having obtained permission, one should never remain even for a single moment in falsehood.
One who keeps the rosary and the ritual components secret, and who knows the divisions of time for the performance of rites,
attains success in due order while wandering through the sacred fields of accomplishment.
Alternatively, having taken possession of a sacred field (kṣetra) presided over by a true emblem (salliṅga), one should dwell there—
[a field] secured by Gaṇeśa, the Bull, Skanda, the Mothers, and Lokeśa.
The gateway to the southern and northern directions is the abode of Śiva, unguarded,
crowded with great people, and far removed from fuel, flowers, kusha grass, and water.
Having completely abandoned all that is accompanied by affliction,
one should undertake the formal acceptance [of a site] at a place where an arrow, a linga, or a self-manifested [linga] exists, frequented by sages and perfected beings.
Either by one’s own self or by one imagined according to the procedure taught in one’s own ritual manual,
[it should be performed] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, especially during the sun’s northern course.
The wise practitioner, being composed, should perform the ritual acquisition on the eighth lunar day;
having first prepared the sacrificial ground, he should worship the garment of Maheśvara.
Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should perform the subsidiary fire-oblation (anuhoma) ten times that amount,
while Śaṃkara resides within the worshipped liṅga, accompanied by abundant garlands, offerings, incense, and other such items.
One should place the lords of the directions, beginning with Śakra, in their respective quarters in the form of spikes;
having joined them together with a thread that has become the channel, one should draw them on the outside.

Reciting the *Māheśvara* weapon-mantra while blazing with ashes, one should surround the enclosure with all the seed-syllables (*bījas*), reciting the armor-mantra (*varma*) as they are applied within it.
One should likewise fashion a wall and armor for one's own abode;
every day at dusk, one should place the world-protectors upon the stakes of the abode.
One should worship those weapons on the outer enclosure, the thick covering within;
and on the festival days, one should worship the Kṣetrapāla in his own directional sector and those situated on the rim of the field.
Whatever is lacking in the field, one should obtain from afar through the assistance of others;
yet, one should not abandon the field of accomplishment and take even a single step elsewhere.
Through one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra according to its color and through a fire sacrifice amounting to one-tenth of that number,
the mantra becomes effective for one who abides by the conduct prescribed in his own scripture.
One who has committed a transgression should perform the expiation as prescribed by the rules;
a wise person should perform that same rite three times over if it was done intentionally rather than unintentionally.
If the daily practice of the practitioner is interrupted, he should recite the Sadyojāta mantra ten thousand times,
or a hundred times with his breath controlled, subsisting on air for the duration of the day.
In the event of an exchange of food with a left-handed person (vāmaka), or when there is violence involving one of manifold forms,
or when [the mantra] flows from the mouth at night, one should recite it twice as much during the day.

In the event of contact with the remnants of food from twice-born men or others, one should worship whichever deity corresponds to the mouth or other part [of the body] within the center of a four-petaled lotus; then, in that location, one should worship the fifth [deity].
Having fasted for six days, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on forest fare;
or, if the transgression is known, one should offer ten thousand oblations, doubling that number for the sake of purification.
If one comes into contact with the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one should recite all the Brahmamantras a hundred thousand times;
if one consumes the remains of offerings, one should recite a hundred thousand times the entire Saṃhitā.
Vāmā and the others are the lords of the Śākyas, the Arthikas, and the Kapālins; Aja is declared to be the sovereign of those who bear the emblems of the triple Veda and the Naiṣṭhikas.
Purification from eating that food is like purification from contact with certain castes;
however, it is held that this occurs at the conclusion of the lunar penance (aindava-vrata) for consuming the food of a Kāpālika.

One should recite the mantra of Īśāna one hundred thousand times for the purification of that mixture; for a mixture involving Kāpālikas, one who has practiced self-restraint should recite it three hundred thousand times.
If the *liṅga* is lost through negligence, or if the rosary (*sākṣasūtra*) has fallen away,
one should recite the mantra of Maheśa one hundred thousand times and then perform the rite of re-acceptance once again.
O Sage, when a downfall or a breach has been committed, a tenth part [of the penance] is prescribed;
in other cases, it is half or a quarter, while for a very minor offense, it is a thousandth part.
And likewise, when [the thread] is seen by an animal, one should recite ten times;
if there is a break in its strands, one should recite half that amount to remove the defect of the counting-thread. (MṛgT 3.117)
And there is discarding [of the food] if one has been touched by phlegm, feces, or urine—except in the case of something metallic;
having approached a woman out of negligence, one should practice ten thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). MṛgT 3.118.
For purification, one should perform ten repetitions multiplied by two (twenty), accompanied by the utterance of the *praṇava*;
in the case of association with a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), it should be joined with eleven repetitions of the name of Śiva.
One who restrains the breath and subsists on fruits and roots should recite [the mantra] ten times;
for those who are equal to him, it shall be exactly the same, but without the restraint of the breath. (MṛgT 3.120)
Regarding other sins and transgressions of ritual action,
one should mutter the *ajāta* mantra eleven times, or once, with the *brahman* placed in the middle.
One should not accept anything brought by a female friend who has incurred sin;
if one accepts it through ignorance, one should perform half of the penance previously mentioned.
In a yoga involving many deities, [the practice] is equal due to the connection with common characteristics;
having understood this, the wise practitioner should resort to an assistant endowed with excellent qualities.
Then, [one should choose] another who is of the same caste and noble birth, younger, superior in qualities, established in the observances, or someone very affectionate toward him. MṛgT 3.124.
The guru who is not under his own control must observe the vow as prescribed by the practitioner;
however, one who is under his own control should observe it for double that duration, while the practitioner who is not under his own control should likewise observe it for that same length of time.
One who is under his own control [may practice] three times [the prescribed amount]; one who is a *putraka* may do so minus one-third;
and a *samayin*, however, may do half of what a *putraka* does—this applies to the aforementioned and unmentioned sins.
The practitioner of mantra, together with his followers, should perform either the *kṛcchra* penance every six months, or annually, or the *aindava*, the *parāka*, or the *taptakṛcchra*. (MṛgT 3.127)
One seeking the accomplishment free from obstacles, and the other three for the sake of liberation— another procedure is declared for them which removes all defects.

That [state] which was obtained by the gods through austerity from Hara for the nourishment of their own practice—whether in the month of Śrāvaṇa, at its conclusion, or in Nabhasya—it is described as follows: MṛgT 3.129.
Having obtained the purifier of Śambhu, one should fulfill the annual rite.
That [image] is made of copper, iron, clay, gems, or wood, and is established on earth;
it is prescribed by the Omniscient One for one who desires worldly enjoyment or for anyone else.
That which is made of jewels should be one finger-breadth up to two cubits in length, but not beyond that;
that made of iron and other metals should be up to six cubits; and that made of wood may be up to three times that length.
